headings.title: Introduction and Etiology of COVID-19
headings.content: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is an infectious respiratory illness caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), a novel enveloped RNA virus belonging to the Coronaviridae family. First identified in Wuhan, China, in late 2019, the virus quickly spread globally, leading to a catastrophic pandemic that challenged healthcare systems worldwide, including resource-limited settings like Nigeria. Structurally, SARS-CoV-2 features prominent surface spike (S) glycoproteins that give the virus its characteristic crown-like appearance under an electron microscope. These spike proteins are vital because they mediate viral entry into host cells by binding specifically to human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors, which are abundantly expressed in the respiratory tract, vascular endothelium, heart, kidneys, and intestines. Understanding the viral etiology is foundational for nursing students, as it dictates how antiviral medications and vaccines interact with the virus. Transmission occurs primarily through respiratory droplets and aerosols expelled when an infected person breathes, talks, coughs, or sneezes, as well as through direct contact with contaminated surfaces followed by touching the face. The incubation period typically ranges from 2 to 14 days, with a median of about 4 to 5 days, during which individuals can be contagious before showing symptoms. As nursing professionals in Nigeria, recognizing these fundamental etiologic and transmission characteristics helps formulate effective public health messaging and guides proper personal protective equipment usage to prevent nosocomial spread in local clinics and tertiary hospitals.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Transmission Dynamics
headings.content: The pathophysiology of COVID-19 begins when the SARS-CoV-2 virus attaches to ACE2 receptors, primarily targeting alveolar epithelial type II cells in the lungs. Once inside, the virus replicates extensively, causing cellular damage, localized inflammation, and apoptosis. This local injury triggers the immune system to recruit macrophages and neutrophils, releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleukins (IL-6, IL-1) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha). In severe cases, this immune response escalates into a dangerous phenomenon known as a 'cytokine storm.' The cytokine storm leads to systemic hyperinflammation, widespread endothelial injury, increased vascular permeability, and pulmonary edema, which impairs gas exchange and culminates in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Transmission dynamics are heavily influenced by viral load, environmental factors, and human behavior. Asymptomatic and presymptomatic carriers play a significant role in spreading the disease because infected individuals can shed high amounts of virus before realizing they are sick. Airborne transmission via aerosols in poorly ventilated indoor spaces poses a major risk, alongside droplet spread via close contact within one to two meters. In densely populated Nigerian settings, such as open markets, public buses (danfos), and crowded wards, these transmission dynamics facilitate rapid outbreaks. Nurses must comprehend these pathophysiological mechanisms and transmission routes to advocate for strict room ventilation, proper masking, and early anti-inflammatory or antiviral interventions for at-risk patients.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Staging
headings.content: Clinical manifestations of COVID-19 are remarkably diverse, ranging from completely asymptomatic infection to critical illness, multi-organ failure, and death. Common symptoms include fever or chills, dry cough, fatigue, shortness of breath, myalgia, headache, sore throat, and the hallmark loss of taste (ageusia) or smell (anosmia). Gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea can also occur. Clinically, COVID-19 is staged into mild, moderate, severe, and critical categories to guide therapeutic management and resource allocation. Mild illness presents with upper respiratory tract symptoms without shortness of breath or abnormal imaging. Moderate illness involves evidence of lower respiratory disease during clinical assessment or imaging, with an oxygen saturation (SpO2) of 93% or higher on room air at sea level. Severe illness is marked by clinical signs of pneumonia plus an SpO2 of less than 93% on room air, a respiratory rate greater than 30 breaths per minute, or lung infiltrates exceeding 50%. Critical illness is defined by the presence of respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, septic shock, and/or multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS). Nigerian nurses working in emergency departments and primary health centers must perform systematic baseline staging using pulse oximetry to quickly identify patients progressing from moderate to severe categories, ensuring timely oxygen therapy escalation.

headings.title: Assessment, Diagnosis, and Triage in Primary Health Care
headings.content: Primary health care (PHC) facilities in Nigeria serve as the first point of contact for individuals presenting with febrile and respiratory illnesses. Effective assessment, diagnosis, and triage protocols are vital to isolate suspected COVID-19 cases immediately and prevent transmission to healthcare workers and other patients. Triage begins at the facility entrance, where patients are screened for respiratory symptoms, fever, and epidemiological risk factors. Suspected cases are escorted to a designated isolation or holding area. Diagnostic confirmation relies primarily on molecular testing using reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) nasopharyngeal swabs, which remain the gold standard. Where RT-PCR is unavailable or turnaround times are delayed, rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) detecting SARS-CoV-2 antigens offer a valuable, cost-effective alternative for quick clinical decision-making at the primary care level. Nursing assessment must include a thorough history, vital signs (specifically measuring room-air oxygen saturation with a pulse oximeter), respiratory effort, and level of consciousness using the AVPU or GCS scale. Nurses must also assess for red flags such as central cyanosis, inability to speak in full sentences, and severe chest pain. Documenting these findings accurately ensures proper referral to secondary or tertiary treatment centers when a patient's condition exceeds the capacity of the primary health clinic.

headings.title: Patient Management and Nursing Care
headings.content: Patient management and nursing care for individuals with COVID-19 require a holistic, multidisciplinary approach focused on supportive care, symptom management, and hemodynamic stabilization. For patients with mild disease managed at home, nurses provide education on hydration, nutrition, fever control with paracetamol, and monitoring warning signs. In hospital settings, oxygen therapy is the cornerstone of management for moderate to severe cases. Nurses must skillfully administer oxygen via nasal cannula, simple face masks, or non-rebreather masks, ensuring target oxygen saturations between 94% and 98% (or 88% to 92% for patients with chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure). Positioning plays a critical role; awake prone positioning (having conscious patients lie on their stomachs) can significantly improve oxygenation and ventilation-perfusion matching in non-intubated patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. Pharmacological management may include corticosteroids (such as dexamethasone) to reduce systemic inflammation, anticoagulants (such as low-molecular-weight heparin) to prevent thromboembolic events, and antiviral medications where indicated. Nursing care also encompasses meticulous skin integrity management for immobilized or proned patients, nutritional support via oral or enteral routes, and psychological support to alleviate the profound anxiety and isolation experienced by hospitalized patients. Monitoring fluid balance, tracking laboratory parameters, and watching for sudden clinical deterioration are daily priorities for the professional nurse.

headings.title: Complications and Long COVID
headings.content: While many individuals recover from acute COVID-19 within weeks, a significant number experience persistent health issues, widely termed Long COVID or post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC). Long COVID is characterized by symptoms that persist or develop weeks or months after the acute infection has resolved, affecting multiple organ systems. Common persistent symptoms include debilitating fatigue, chronic cough, shortness of breath, chest pain, cognitive dysfunction ('brain fog'), sleep disturbances, joint pain, and anxiety or depression. The exact pathophysiology remains under investigation, but theories include persistent tissue reservoirs of the virus, immune system dysregulation, autoimmunity, and microvascular thrombosis. Additionally, acute COVID-19 patients are at elevated risk for serious immediate and subacute complications, including pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, stroke, myocardial injury, and secondary bacterial or fungal infections like pulmonary aspergillosis. Nursing students must recognize that recovery from COVID-19 does not end at hospital discharge. Nurses play a crucial role in post-COVID care clinics by screening for lingering physical and psychological deficits, coordinating multidisciplinary rehabilitation (such as physical therapy and pulmonary exercises), offering empathetic counseling, and supporting patients as they slowly reintegrate into their work and community life in Nigeria.

headings.title: Infection Prevention and Control Measures
headings.content: Infection prevention and control (IPC) measures are the bedrock of stopping the spread of SARS-CoV-2 in healthcare settings and communities. Standard, contact, and airborne precautions must be rigorously implemented whenever caring for suspected or confirmed COVID-19 patients. Hand hygiene using soap and water or alcohol-based hand rub is mandatory before and after patient contact. Personal protective equipment (PPE)—including medical masks or N95 respirators, face shields or goggles, gowns, and gloves—must be worn correctly, with strict adherence to proper donning and doffing techniques to avoid self-contamination. Aerosol-generating procedures (AGPs), such as endotracheal intubation, suctioning, and nebulizer therapy, require airborne precautions in adequately ventilated rooms or negative-pressure isolation spaces. Environmental cleaning and disinfection of high-touch surfaces using chlorine-based solutions or hospital-grade disinfectants are critical routines for nurses to oversee in Nigerian wards. Furthermore, healthcare worker surveillance, prompt testing of staff with symptoms, and adherence to quarantine guidelines protect the medical workforce from depletion during waves of infection. Nurses act as IPC champions, educating patients, visitors, and junior staff on infection control protocols to foster a safe healing environment.

headings.title: Community Surveillance and Vaccination Strategies
headings.content: Community surveillance and vaccination strategies are essential public health pillars for controlling COVID-19 transmission on a population level, particularly in Nigeria. Community surveillance involves active case finding, contact tracing, and genomic sequencing to monitor local infection trends and detect emerging variants of concern (VOCs). Public health nurses often lead community sensitization campaigns, dispelling myths and encouraging individuals to report symptoms early and get tested. Vaccination is proven to be the most effective strategy for preventing severe disease, hospitalization, and death from COVID-19. Global and national vaccine rollout programs utilize various platforms, including mRNA vaccines, viral vector vaccines, and inactivated virus vaccines, to stimulate durable adaptive immunity by prompting the production of neutralizing antibodies and T-cell responses. In Nigeria, overcoming vaccine hesitancy is a major hurdle that requires culturally sensitive communication, community leader engagement, and accessible mobile vaccination drives. Nurses play an indispensable advocacy and delivery role by educating the public on vaccine safety, managing minor adverse effects, debunking misinformation on social media, and ensuring equitable vaccine distribution across urban slums and remote rural communities.
